answer: This is in scope, and it is exactly the pattern CRMsci was extended to cover. The pinned moth stays what it always was: an E20 Biological Object, identified by its original catalogue number, merely diminished by having a leg removed -- it is not destroyed and does not change identity. The clipping-and-extraction is an activity of CRMsci's S1 Matter Removal branch, specifically S2 Sample Taking (a subclass of S1, and S1 is declared superclass of both S2 and E80 Part Removal) -- S2's own scope note says the removed matter 'may acquire a persistent identity of different nature beyond the act of its removal, such as becoming a physical object in the narrower sense', and S1's scope note gives the identical instruction: model this by multiple instantiation, not by stretching the source's identity onto the removed matter. Concretely: O3 sampled from links the S2 Sample Taking event to the moth (S10 Material Substantial is CRMsci's declared superclass of E18, so the moth qualifies as source), and O5 removed links the same event to the resulting new item, an S13 Sample -- which, once the tissue is dissolved into a frozen extract, is itself a distinct persistent thing under its own new catalogue number. So the honest answer to the case's first question is: the extract should be recorded as a new object brought into existence by a sampling event that also diminished (not destroyed) the original specimen -- not as 'a part removed... using the specimen's existing identity'; the two objects are not the same thing wearing two labels. On the second question -- whether the extract still counts as coming from the paratype -- the SIG's own resolution of Issue 332 answers this directly: a sub-sample is normally given a new identifier and 'we cannot guarantee that the identity condition remains after splitting the sample. A sub-sample is always different to the original sample' (issue332#current-s0012), but in the same breath: 'Provenance can be tracked through the sampling events' (issue332#current-s0012). So identity is not preserved (the extract is not the paratype), but provenance is not lost either -- the O3 sampled from / O5 removed chain is exactly the mechanism for asserting 'this extract was taken from the specimen that carries paratype status' without claiming the extract shares that specimen's identity or catalogue number.

rejected_alternatives.option: E80 Part Removal alone, with the extract carried under the moth's existing identifier
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E80's own scope note only supports keeping a single identity when the removed part has no separate documentary role; here the removed matter is explicitly given its own new catalogue number and further processed (dissolved) into an extract, which is precisely the case S1 Matter Removal's scope note redirects to 'multiple instantiation with adequate concepts of creating the respective items' rather than treating it as one continuous identity.

rejected_alternatives.option: Treating the extract as the same object as the moth (shared identity, no new item)
rejected_alternatives.why_not: Issue 332's resolution states outright that 'we cannot guarantee that the identity condition remains after splitting the sample. A sub-sample is always different to the original sample' and that in practice 'a sub-sample is normally given a new identifier' (issue332#current-s0011/s0012) -- which is also simply what the case already describes happening (a new catalogue number).

rejected_alternatives.option: E81 Transformation of the whole moth
rejected_alternatives.why_not: E81 (and E80/S1's own scope notes) reserve that reading for cases where 'the whole ceases to exist' or is totally decomposed; the moth remains in its drawer under its original number, missing only a leg, so it is diminished (P112/E80 or the CRMsci S1 branch), not transformed or destroyed.
